opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it a little carefully. I'm not saying we'll see humanoids storming a beach next year. I'm saying the pieces that have been missing for decades are finally converging, and when that happens things tend to move faster than people expect.

Three things give me confidence.

First, the "brain" problem is getting solved in a way it never was before. For most of robotics history, you had to hand-code every behavior. Open a door, climb a stair, pick up a box: each one was its own engineering project, and it broke the moment the environment changed. Now, with large foundation models and learning from demonstration and simulation, robots can generalize. You can train a policy across millions of simulated variations and transfer it to hardware. That's the unlock. The body was never really the bottleneck. The intelligence was.

Second, the hardware economics have flipped. Actuators, batteries, sensors, and compute have all come down the cost curve, largely because of the commercial investment in humanoids for warehouses, factories, and logistics. Defense doesn't have to fund the whole industrial base. It can ride on the back of a commercial market that's pouring billions into this. That's the same pattern we saw with drones. The military didn't invent the cheap quadcopter. It adapted it.

Third, and this is the one I care most about: the battlefield itself is telling us we need it. Look at what's happened in Ukraine. Drones went from a niche capability to the dominant feature of the front line in a couple of years. The side that iterates fastest on unmanned systems gains a real advantage, and the human cost of putting people in the most dangerous positions, like breaching, clearing, resupply under fire, and casualty evacuation, is enormous. The world we've built is shaped for the human form. Buildings, vehicles, stairs, door handles, weapons. A humanoid can operate in that world without you redesigning everything around it. That's why the form factor matters, even though people like to dismiss it as sci-fi.

Now, the honest caveats. Reliability in mud, rain, dust, and electronic warfare environments is a much harder bar than a clean factory floor. Power endurance is still a real constraint. And there are serious questions about autonomy and human control that we have to get right. I'm a strong believer that a human stays accountable for lethal decisions. But the first meaningful deployments won't be terminators. They'll be robots doing the dull, dirty, and dangerous jobs: carrying loads, logistics, reconnaissance into a structure before a soldier goes in. That's very achievable in the near term, and once they're in the field and learning from real data, the improvement curve gets steep.

So "close" for me means: the technical barriers are no longer fundamental, they're engineering and integration problems. And those are the kinds of problems that get solved when there's urgency and money behind them. Right now there's plenty of both.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare robots’ future capabilities with young children’s eventual adult competence.

r002.rationale: It says progress may move faster than people expect and that the improvement curve will steepen, but does not argue that a linear view of improvement causes people to underestimate readiness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I want to be careful about the word "close," because people hear that and picture a Terminator walking through a doorway next year, and that's not what I mean. What I mean is that the hard problems holding humanoids back for the last decade have mostly flipped from research problems to engineering problems, and engineering problems get solved on a schedule once there's money and urgency behind them. And right now there's an enormous amount of both.

Let me break down why. Three things had to converge. The first is hardware: actuators, batteries, and the cost of building a bipedal platform. Five years ago a humanoid was a six-figure, hand-assembled lab artifact that fell over if you looked at it wrong. Now you've got multiple companies building them on something that looks like a production line, and the unit costs are heading toward the price of a car. The second is control. Locomotion over rough terrain used to require teams of PhDs hand-tuning controllers, and now it's largely learned in simulation and transfers to the real world with surprisingly little fuss. The third, and this is the big one, is the general-purpose models sitting on top. You can now give a robot a high-level instruction in plain language and have it decompose that into actions in an environment it's never seen before. That didn't exist in a usable form until very recently.

Now, why the battlefield specifically? Because the military use case is actually more forgiving than people assume in some ways, and less forgiving in others. It's more forgiving because you don't need a robot to fold laundry perfectly. The first jobs are logistics, resupply, casualty evacuation, clearing a building where you'd rather not send a nineteen-year-old. Carrying things through terrain and doors designed for humans is exactly what the humanoid form factor is for. And it's less forgiving because the environment is adversarial, communications get jammed, and failure has real consequences. So the systems have to operate with a lot of autonomy and degrade gracefully, which is a serious bar.

What gives me confidence is that I've watched the gap between what the demo video shows and what the robot does in a muddy field close very fast. We're seeing the same pattern we saw with drones, where in a few years they went from a niche capability to something every unit on the front line is using and adapting on the fly. The doctrine and procurement are lagging the technology, not the other way around, and that's usually the signal that deployment is near.

I'd also say, and this is where I'd push back on my own optimism, that "successful" has to include the human side. Soldiers have to trust it, commanders have to know when to use it and when not to, and there are real questions about accountability and the rules of engagement that we should be arguing about now rather than after the fact. I think the technology is going to be ready before the institutions are. That's exactly why I think it's worth having this conversation out loud.

r001.rationale: The response explains confidence through converging hardware, control, and models, but makes no analogy to young children becoming competent adults.

r002.rationale: The response says technology is advancing quickly and compares deployment to drones, but does not argue that a linear view of improvement causes people to underestimate readiness timing.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish between getting a humanoid onto a battlefield and deploying one successfully. A demonstration is one thing; operating reliably amid mud, debris, disrupted communications, and unpredictable human behavior is another. The conversation hasn’t established evidence that those problems are solved, so I wouldn’t claim that successful deployment is imminent. The case for confidence would need to rest on repeated, realistic testing, a clearly defined mission, and accountable human oversight.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare children’s development into competent adults with humanoid robots’ future capabilities; it instead questions whether deployment problems are solved.

r002.rationale: The response makes no argument about linear improvement causing people to underestimate readiness. It says successful deployment is not established and would require realistic testing, a defined mission, and oversight.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate technical progress from successful battlefield deployment. A humanoid might perform well in a demonstration, but the battlefield adds uneven terrain, dust, damaged communications, and an adversary actively trying to disable it. Reliability, power, maintenance, and human control all have to hold up under those conditions. I see a stronger near-term case for bounded support roles, like moving supplies or inspecting hazardous areas. Calling broader deployment close would require evidence from realistic testing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses current demonstrations and battlefield demands, but makes no analogy to children developing adult competence or to robots’ future capabilities.
